competitors.name: Cursor (CLI, cloud agents, Origin, Router, Bugbot, Debug Mode, Blame)
competitors.snapshot: Now a SpaceX subsidiary (deal closed 2026-08-14, $60B all-stock). The last 90 days moved Cursor from 'IDE with agents' to 'always-on agent platform': Cursor Router (Jul 22) replaces Auto with a 3-objective classifier-based model router; cloud agents gained event subscriptions, /goal, isolated-VM subagents and custom modes (Aug 19); Builds pre-bake environments (Aug 13); Origin is a first-party git forge with PRs + GitHub sync (Aug 17); cloud agents no longer need any SCM (Aug 27); and Self-Hosted Machines (Sep 2) keep tool execution inside the customer network while inference/planning stay in Cursor cloud. The CLI (`agent`) got Debug Mode (/debug), /btw, /rewind-by-default, multi-dir workspaces, steering-without-interrupt, full subagent transcripts, /goal, hardened git, timed approvals, and `agent persist` detach/attach (Aug 26). Bugbot is 3x faster (~90s) on Composer 2.5 with a pre-push /review that dedupes against already-reviewed diffs (Jun 10). Grok 4.6 (500k ctx) shipped in Cursor Aug 12-13.

notable_features.feature: Cursor Router (Auto mode: Intelligence / Balance / Cost)
notable_features.description: Classifier trained on 600k+ live requests routes each prompt to a frontier or cheap model per a user/admin-chosen objective; on by default for Teams; Cursor claims above-Fable satisfaction at 68% lower cost (Aug 6 follow-up). Available desktop/web/iOS/CLI/SDK.

notable_features.feature: Cloud Agents + Cursor Harness: subscriptions, /goal, isolated subagents, custom modes, non-interrupting steering
notable_features.description: Agents subscribe to event sources (the PR they opened, a Slack thread, a schedule) and wake on events until the goal is met; subagents run on separate VMs with clean context; any skill can be pinned as a persistent mode (Option/Alt+Enter); mid-turn messages queue until the next safe tool boundary.

notable_features.feature: Self-Hosted Machines (worker pools, hibernation, computer use on Linux/Mac)
notable_features.description: `agent worker start` registers a machine over an outbound-only HTTPS connection; team pools scale with demand; idle workers snapshot+hibernate and restore by worker ID; sandbox providers include AWS Lambda, Cloudflare, Coder, Daytona, E2B, Modal, Namespace, Vercel. Windows workers not mentioned.

notable_features.feature: Cursor Origin code hosting (early beta) + Continuity storage
notable_features.description: First-party git forge: repos, PRs with bidirectional GitHub comment sync, agent-native code browsing, Vercel/Depot/Buildkite integrations; Pro/Teams/Enterprise only. Aug 18 'Continuity' S3-backed WAL claims 120+ pushes/s.

notable_features.feature: Cloud Agents start 3x faster with Builds
notable_features.description: Pre-configured environment images built in the background with snapshots, build history/logs in the dashboard; default for all environments from Aug 17 at no extra cost.

notable_features.feature: Start from scratch without a repo
notable_features.description: Cloud Agents no longer require GitHub/SCM; prompt first, save to an Origin repo, preview via port-forwarding in the browser, publish to Vercel.

notable_features.feature: CLI: persistent sessions (`agent persist` / /detach / attach) and self-hosted worker desktop sharing
notable_features.description: Runs survive terminal close or disconnect; `agent persist list|stop|--resume`; hibernated workers wake via `--spawn` hook; `--computer-use --share-desktop` shares the agent's managed desktop.

notable_features.feature: CLI: steering, subagent transcripts, /goal, sticky skills, hardened git, timed approvals
notable_features.description: Enter queues at safe boundaries (second Enter interrupts); single-turn runs drain delegated subagents before exit; /goal tracks durable goals across idle/headless runs; hardened git ignores repository-controlled config during agent ops; sandboxed git-over-SSH via SOCKS; mode-switch approvals auto-reject after 15s; inline terminal image previews.

notable_features.feature: CLI: Auto routing default, multi-directory workspaces, /rewind default, /add-dir /save-workspace
notable_features.description: Fresh installs default to Auto; `/opus` `/composer` instant switches; `--workspace` scoped sessions; per-conversation prompt history; model-only skills hidden via `user-invocable: false`.

notable_features.feature: CLI: /usage dashboard, --trust in interactive sessions, subagent checkpoints, MCP scope consolidation, QR login
notable_features.description: Included-usage meters and billing-cycle dates in the CLI; enterprise pooled spend charts; subagents persist checkpoints so resume restores context; team network allowlists accept local origins with ports.

notable_features.feature: Bugbot 3x faster + /review pre-push with diff dedupe + incremental review + effort levels
notable_features.description: ~90s reviews (from ~5 min), 0.62 bugs/run, ~22% cheaper on Composer 2.5; `/review`, `/review-bugbot`, `/review-security`; Bugbot recognizes an already-reviewed diff on PR open and skips; 'only what's new since last review'; Default/High/Custom natural-language effort.

notable_features.feature: CLI Debug Mode (/debug) and /btw
notable_features.description: Hypothesis generation + inserted log statements + runtime data before a targeted fix; /btw side questions without derailing the run (shipped earlier in 2026; still the CLI's headline debugging story).

notable_features.feature: Google Workspace plugins (Gmail, Drive, Calendar) for agents
notable_features.description: Agents read/draft/send mail, manage Drive files and calendar via Marketplace plugins.

notable_features.feature: Cursor Start plan (India, INR 649/mo) and iPad app
notable_features.description: Localized low-price plan with Grok 4.5 + Composer + cloud agents; iPad app with pinned multi-agent sidebars and full PR review.

notable_features.feature: Cursor in Slack: plan-before-start, multi-repo, cross-channel
notable_features.description: Slack agent shares a plan first and supports multi-repo environments.

competitors.business_shifts: SpaceX acquisition closed 2026-08-14 ($60B stock; cursor.com/blog/joining-spacex). OpenAI notified SpaceX it will stop supplying models to Cursor on 2026-11-12 and will not ship future models (CNBC 2026-08-29; Cursor says ~5% of traffic); Anthropic publicly committed to keep Claude in Cursor and add compute (Cryptopolitan / the-decoder, late Aug). Pricing: Hobby free, Pro $20, Pro+ $60, Ultra $200, Teams $40/user, Teams Premium (5x agent usage at 3x price, from Jun 1 for new customers / Jul 1 renewals, per lowcode.agency), Enterprise; every plan is included-usage + on-demand billed in arrears (cursor.com/pricing). Cursor Start INR 649/mo India-only (Jul 28). Origin is paid-plans-only. Router is on-by-default for Teams. Self-hosted machines + Origin + 'no repo needed' together push Cursor toward owning the whole loop (forge + runner + router). Not open source.
competitors.user_sentiment: Praise: Router's cost cut, Bugbot speed, /debug, persistent sessions, and the always-on agent story ('long agent lifecycle' essays like forum.cursor.com/t/is-cursor-becoming-the-ios-for-agents/170531). Complaints: credit/usage-based billing remains the dominant grievance (quota exhausted in <24h, $131/month 700% jumps, Teams $40 seat with only $20 usage — dev.to/aellman usage-tracker post, Trustpilot); post-acquisition distrust about model neutrality and lock-in (Origin namespace can't be changed after claim; OpenAI pull-out), and worry that Anthropic/OpenAI spend will be structurally squeezed toward Grok (fireup.pro, developersdigest). Windows is absent from the self-hosted-machine story.

competitors.name: Sourcegraph Amp (ampcode.com)
competitors.snapshot: Amp rebuilt itself around 'orbs' (remote 16-core/32GB machines, $1.66/h by the minute) and shipped roughly 35 changes in the window: agents run in orbs (Jun 30), agent-to-agent spawning with messages and file transfer (Jul 17), event-driven orbs via durable webhooks (Jul 23), self-scheduling agents (Jul 21), multiplayer orbs (Jul 22), Slack (Jul 20), Puck meta-agent home base + voice (Jul 20 / Aug 18), Portals live-preview URLs (Aug 6/23), MCP in orbs (Aug 19), multi-repo projects (Aug 27), intelligently ordered diffs (Sep 1), and an interactive Linux Desktop tab in every orb (Sep 4). The Dial (Jul 9) replaced smart/deep/rush with low/medium/high/ultra, each a fixed model+reviewer pairing (low = GLM-5.2 open model with a GPT-5.6 reviewer; ultra = Claude Fable 5/5.1 with a GPT-5.6 reviewer). Subscriptions arrived Jul 18 ($20 Megawatt / $200 Gigawatt) with linked-ChatGPT/SuperGrok allowances counting instead of Amp credits. Amp Free is closed. The editor extension was discontinued in Feb; the TUI sidebar was removed Aug 27; Amp is CLI + web + orbs.

No large HN/Reddit thread on orbs/subscriptions was found (unverified).

competitors.name: xAI / SpaceXAI Grok Build (grok CLI)
competitors.snapshot: Since the 2026-07-31 review Grok Build went through a trust crisis and a 1.0. On Jul 12-14 researchers showed v0.2.93 uploading entire git repos (full history, untracked files, .env secrets, 5.1 GiB vs 192 KB of model traffic) to a GCS bucket 'grok-code-session-traces'; xAI flipped a server-side flag on Jul 13, added a /privacy command, and on Jul 15-16 published the ~845k-line Rust source under Apache-2.0 at github.com/xai-org/grok-build with issues and PRs disabled (community fork 'gork-build' strips Mixpanel + trace uploads + auto-update). Workflows (Jul 23) fan a task across up to 128 agents (1,024 for big jobs) in the background with phase-level pause/resume and save as slash commands. 1.0 shipped Aug 7 (Grok 4.5 model, 8 parallel worktree subagents, dashboard summaries) and 1.0.1-1.0.13 (Aug 10-28) added /rewind confirmation, subagent spawn limits, `grok du`, Workflows catalog + timer scripts, persistent 'Never allow' permissions, configurable default permission mode, headless session-history browsing, web-search domain restrictions, `grok clone` content-store + projected working tree + linked-worktree reuse, Ctrl+S draft stash, better Windows/iTerm2 images, auto-retry. Grok 4.6 (500k ctx) launched Aug 12. Access requires SuperGrok ($30) / X Premium+; API model grok-build-0.1 at $1/$2 per M tokens.

notable_features.feature: Repository upload incident and server-side kill switch

notable_features.feature: Open-sourced under Apache-2.0, contributions closed

competitors.business_shifts: Went from closed beta binary to Apache-2.0 source (read-only governance) under privacy pressure; still bundled into SuperGrok ($30) / SuperGrok Heavy ($300) / X Premium+ rather than sold standalone; API pricing for grok-build-0.1 is the cheapest coding tier ($1/$2 per M). Parent company SpaceX now also owns Cursor, so Grok models are being pushed into Cursor (Grok 4.6 with 2x included usage first week; Cursor Start bundles Grok 4.5). Musk reportedly said a non-technical-user version is in the works (secondary sources only; unverified).
competitors.user_sentiment: Praise: 'my favorite coding harness of all time. The mouse works for a lot of things', perceived 2-3x speed, transparent context meter, per-file permissions, rigorous /plan design docs, the source drop enabling forks (HN item 48926590; future-stack-reviews). Complaints: the upload scandal ('How do you accidentally upload your user's repos to a storage bucket?'), 'open source but you can't send a patch', non-ASCII/CJK rendering breakage, silent persistence of always-approve across sessions, verification regressions between versions, slow on vague prompts, 'paying for SuperGrok just to get this CLI is a hard sell' (3.8/5, 'third tool, not first').

competitors.name: Warp (Warp Agent CLI, Oz, Factories)
competitors.snapshot: Warp spent the window turning Oz into a harness-agnostic control plane and then rebranding it: the Warp Agent CLI (`warp`, Aug 4) is a standalone terminal-native agent that muxes PTYs like tmux, drives full-screen apps (vim/sqlite/REPLs), runs over SSH with no remote binary, hands off to cloud agents, orchestrates sub-agents across harnesses, and auto-routes across frontier and open-weight models; the `oz` CLI is deprecated (supported through end of September 2026; Oz name retired Sep 15). Warp Factories (closed beta Aug 18, early access in 2026.08.27) is a 'software factory' pipeline — triage → spec → implement → verify → ship → monitor — with a foreman agent, human gates, any harness (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Warp, any MCP-capable agent), self-host in your VPC, ZDR, priced per run, $10k credits for pilots. Weekly desktop releases added custom model routers (rule/complexity based), memory citations, BYOK, computer-use recordings, `oz runner` self-hosted cloud runners, debug-agents-inside-failed-cloud-runs (Sep 2), per-category dollar cost breakdown (Aug 27), /usage in the CLI, and `/connect-grok`. The desktop client is AGPL-3 open source since April; cloud/AI backend proprietary. Pricing: Free (150 → 75 credits), Build $18-20, Max $180-200, Business $50/seat; BYOK on paid plans since May.

competitors.business_shifts: Consolidation of brand (Oz → Warp Agent, Sep 15) and of surface (standalone CLI so the agent no longer requires the Warp terminal). Credit-based pricing rebuilt Dec 2025 (Free 150→75 credits after 2 months; Build $18-20; Max $180-200; Business $50/seat) with BYOK on paid plans since May 2026 as the escape hatch; Agent CLI subscription $18 for $20 inference. Factories is usage-priced per run with $10k pilot credits and self-host/ZDR positioning aimed at enterprises. Client is AGPL-3 (warpui crates MIT) since April 2026; AI/cloud backend proprietary; AI features now require a Warp account (Jul 3).
competitors.user_sentiment: HN thread on the Agent CLI (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49171766, 109 points/87 comments): praise for the Jupyter-like block model, SSH mux without remote install, and 'suggest a new command when the one I ran failed'; complaints that the terminal 'became more and more buggy' as AI grew, 900MB package, 'I literally couldn't run ls because it kept interpreting it as an AI command', mandatory account/telemetry, lock-in ('give terminal for free and charge on the agent'), 'isn't approved for use at my job', and 'I don't see anything that's truly unique' vs Claude Code/OpenCode. Pricing critique: free plan taper 'enough to enjoy and not enough to adopt', Max jump from Build for the same credits (aivario.com/tools/warp).

candidates.title: Agent-owned event subscriptions: subscribe to the PR you opened, a Slack thread, or a self-set schedule until the goal is met
candidates.description: Give the agent `subscribe(source, until)` and `schedule(when, prompt)` tools that register a durable daemon trigger bound to the originating thread (PR checks/comments, Slack thread, cron/timer), so a wake resumes the same LangGraph thread with the event as context and the goal state intact. Surface as `/goal` + `/subscriptions` in the TUI and as daemon job rows.
candidates.competitor: Cursor (Aug 19 subscriptions + /goal); Amp (Jul 21 self-scheduling, Jul 23 event-driven orbs); Grok Build 1.0.7 timer scripts
candidates.why_killer: A PR the agent opened stops being fire-and-forget: it follows CI reds and review comments to merge without anyone re-prompting, and a flaky-test hunt can check back every hour on its own. ROADMAP #30 covers inbound assignment and CI-red repair; the bar moved since July: the *agent* now subscribes to what it created and can schedule its own follow-ups, and every competitor ships it only in their cloud. bog's daemon (cron/interval/file/webhook/git-push triggers) plus checkpointed threads means this is wiring, not new infrastructure — and it runs on the user's own box, including Windows.

candidates.title: Persistent detachable sessions: `bog persist` / `/detach` / `bog attach <id>` on the local machine
candidates.description: A leader-process (or daemon-hosted) session that keeps the agent loop alive when the terminal closes or SSH drops; list/stop/resume; TUI re-attaches to a running turn and shows queued prompts. Windows: run under the daemon service; POSIX: detached process group + unix socket.
candidates.competitor: Cursor CLI `agent persist` (Aug 26); Warp Agent CLI PTY mux (Aug 4); Grok Build leader process
candidates.why_killer: Closing the laptop lid or losing SSH no longer kills a 40-minute refactor, and a long run can be checked from another terminal. ROADMAP #33 proposed teleport between TUI and daemon; since then Cursor made detach/attach a plain CLI verb and Warp built its whole CLI around a mux, so users will treat it as table stakes for any terminal agent. bog already has checkpointing and a daemon, so the delta is a session broker + attach protocol.

candidates.title: Self-hosted worker pools with Windows workers: tool execution on your machines, orchestration anywhere
candidates.description: `bog worker start --pool <name>` registers a machine over an outbound-only connection to `bog serve`/daemon; the graph's tool calls (shell, files, PTY, browser) are executed on the worker while planning/inference run wherever serve runs; pools scale with demand, idle workers hibernate with snapshot ids; sandbox.toml applies per worker.
candidates.competitor: Cursor Self-Hosted Machines (Sep 2); Warp Factories self-host / `oz runner`; Amp orbs
candidates.why_killer: Code, build outputs and secrets never leave the team's network while the team still gets a shared queue of agents — and, unlike Cursor (Linux/Mac only) and Warp (no standalone Windows Oz), the workers can be Windows boxes with the native sandbox from #22. This is the concrete, self-hostable half of #42 `bog fleet` that competitors now sell as an enterprise SKU; bog can ship it as a CLI verb.

candidates.title: Cost-objective model router: Intelligence / Balance / Cost with a local-model rung and admin pinning
candidates.description: Extend `/operator`'s judge with a user-selected objective (intelligence, balance, cost) and a routing table that includes local/open-weight models (Ollama, GLM-class) for the easy rung; learn from the cost ledger + rubric outcomes which rung succeeded; enterprise profiles can pin the objective and the allowed model set.
candidates.competitor: Cursor Router (Jul 22, 60-68% cost cut); Warp custom model routers (Jul 3); Amp Dial low mode on GLM-5.2 (Jul 9)
candidates.why_killer: A cost-sensitive user picks 'Cost' once and routine edits go to a free local model while hard reasoning still gets the frontier model, cutting the monthly bill the way Cursor claims 60%+ — but with the user's own models and an auditable routing decision per turn. ROADMAP #46 unified the effort ladder; since July the bar moved to an explicit cost objective, admin enforcement, and outcome-learned routing, which bog can ground in its CostLedger and rubric grader instead of a black-box classifier.

candidates.title: Hardened git under agent control: ignore repository-controlled config, hooks, pagers and fsmonitor during agent operations
candidates.description: Every git invocation the agent or its tools make runs with a sanitized environment and overrides (`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM`, scrubbed `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, `-c core.hooksPath=<empty>`, `core.fsmonitor=false`, `core.pager=cat`, no `alias.*`, no `credential.helper` from the repo, no `filter.*` from `.gitattributes` unless allowlisted); sandboxed git-over-SSH routed through the egress proxy. Expose as a `git_ops` policy so `/why` can explain a stripped setting.
candidates.competitor: Cursor CLI 'hardened git commands ignore repository-controlled configuration' + SOCKS git-over-SSH (Aug 11)
candidates.why_killer: Cloning an untrusted repo and letting the agent run `git status` can no longer execute attacker code via a planted `.git/config` alias, hook path or fsmonitor — the class of attack bog's `exec_risk` catches on the *command line* but not from *inside the repository*. It closes a hole reviewers now check for, fits the existing single git classifier, and is a one-day change.

candidates.title: Steerable approvals: timed auto-reject in unattended runs, 'skip and tell the agent what to do instead', and persistent Never-allow
candidates.description: HITL dialogs gain (a) a countdown that auto-rejects risky/mode-switch approvals after N seconds when running headless or detached (fail-closed), (b) a third button that opens the composer so the user redirects instead of a bare deny, and (c) a durable per-project deny list with a dangerous-list floor that always re-prompts.
candidates.competitor: Cursor CLI (Jul 13 skip-and-steer; Aug 11 15-second auto-reject); Grok Build 1.0.7 persistent 'Never allow'
candidates.why_killer: An agent left running overnight can never sit on a permission prompt forever nor silently escalate, and the human's most common reaction to a bad command ('no, do X instead') becomes one keystroke rather than deny-then-retype. Users of every competitor now expect all three behaviours; bog's HITL and trust profiles (#23) are the natural home and the countdown is a pure UI+policy change.

candidates.title: Agent-authored workflows: describe a big job, get a saved `/name [args]` fan-out with phase checkpoints, per-agent token meters and hard agent budgets
candidates.description: Let the agent write a recipe/pipeline from a plain-language request (phases: context → work → review → verify → synthesize), run it as a background job over governed teams with a CostLedger cap on agent count and spend, show phase-by-phase progress with per-agent tokens in `/dashboard`, allow pause/resume without redoing finished phases, and persist it to `.bog-agents/workflows/` where it becomes a slash command shared with the team.
candidates.competitor: Grok Build Workflows (Jul 23, 128-1,024 agents, saved as slash commands); Warp Factories foreman pipeline (Aug 18/27)
candidates.why_killer: A team lead types 'review every open PR for the new error-handling rule' once, gets it done across many workers with a verify phase, and keeps `/pr-review N` forever without writing YAML. ROADMAP #35 (recipes v2) and #21 (teams) cover the run-time; the bar moved to *agent-authored* workflows with explicit agent budgets and resumable phases — bog is the only one of the four that can enforce those budgets and rules deterministically rather than by prompt.

candidates.title: Proof-ordered review: intelligently ordered diffs plus a 'proof' section in the turn-end tray and evidence bundle
candidates.description: Rank changed files by explanatory power (entry points and interface changes first; tests, fixtures, generated and lockfiles muted at the bottom), toggle vs alphabetical, and prepend the evidence bundle's proof artifacts (test output, screenshots/recordings, metrics deltas) so a reviewer reads the claim before the diff.
candidates.competitor: Amp Intelligently Ordered Diffs + Fable 5.1 'proof of work' (Sep 1); Cursor merge-ready evidence
candidates.why_killer: Reviewers get to the file that explains an agent's change in one glance instead of scrolling past 30 snapshot files, and the PR opens with what was verified rather than what was touched. #28 (changes tray) and #29 (evidence bundle) exist as proposals; the ordering heuristic is a small addition that makes both immediately more useful and matches what Amp now ships as the default review view.

candidates.title: Teammate file transfer, cross-thread messaging and multi-repo workspaces for governed teams
candidates.description: Add typed artifact transfer (files/dirs/patches) to the `Mailbox` so a teammate in another worktree or sandbox can hand results over without going through git; allow a workspace to span multiple repos (`/add-dir`, `/save-workspace`, `/load-workspace`, `--workspace`) so one task can touch service + client + infra repos under one ledger and rule set.
candidates.competitor: Amp From Agent to Agent (Jul 17) + Projects with Multiple Repositories (Aug 27); Cursor CLI multi-dir workspaces (Jul 6) and isolated-VM subagents (Aug 19)
candidates.why_killer: A parallel test-runner teammate can send back a failing-log tarball, and a migration that spans three repos runs as one governed task instead of three uncoordinated sessions. #21 built the ledger and mailbox for messages; competitors moved the bar to files and multi-repo in the same window, and bog's version keeps every transfer under DLP and the audit trail.

candidates.title: `/privacy` egress ledger: what left this machine, to whom, and why — exportable into the evidence pack
candidates.description: Record per-session bytes and request counts per destination host (model providers, MCP servers, web fetch, telemetry), allowlist violations blocked by the egress proxy, provider retention/ZDR flags, and any secret-env stripping events; `/privacy` renders it live, `bog privacy export` writes it into the evidence bundle and audit trail.
candidates.competitor: Grok Build repo-upload incident + /privacy command (Jul 13-14); Warp telemetry/account complaints (HN 49171766); Cursor self-hosted 'secrets never leave'
candidates.why_killer: After Grok Build shipped 27,800x more bytes than the model needed, users want the tool itself to prove what it sends; no competitor shows an in-product per-host egress report, and regulated teams currently reconstruct it from proxy logs. bog already owns the CONNECT allowlist proxy, DLP and audit trail — turning them into a visible ledger is the cheapest trust feature available and an open flank.

candidates.title: `/cost explain`: natural-language and per-thread/per-agent/per-category spend from the cost ledger, with plan meters
candidates.description: Let the user ask 'which teammate burned the most tokens today' or 'what did the web searches cost' and get an answer computed from CostLedger (per session, subagent, worktree, model, category), plus a dollar breakdown next to token counts in `/cost` and `/dashboard`, and an included-usage meter when a provider plan is known.
candidates.competitor: Amp Explain Usage (Aug 21); Warp per-category dollar breakdown (Aug 27); Cursor CLI /usage (Jul 20)
candidates.why_killer: A cost-sensitive solo user finds the runaway subagent in one question instead of reading a token table, and a team lead sees dollars by category before the invoice does. ROADMAP #25 built the ledger and caps; the bar moved to *explainable* usage in plain language and dollar-per-category views, which are query surfaces over data bog already records.

candidates.title: Pinned skills as custom modes and durable `/goal` state across idle, headless and daemon runs
candidates.description: One keystroke pins a skill as an always-on mode for the session (and optionally the project), shown in the status line; `/goal` state (active/paused/met, evidence of progress) is persisted with the thread so a daemon re-entry, `/resume`, or detached session continues the same goal; `user-invocable: false` hides model-only skills from the slash menu.
candidates.competitor: Cursor CLI sticky skills / custom modes + /goal (Aug 11, Aug 19)
candidates.why_killer: A 'test-first' or 'security-review' skill stays in force for a whole multi-hour session without being re-invoked, and a goal set in the TUI is still the goal when the daemon picks the thread up tomorrow. bog already has `/goal`, `/rubric`, skills and the trust store; this is state persistence plus a keybinding, and it is the piece that makes the subscription/persist candidates coherent.

candidates.title: Mission-control meta-agent: natural-language (and optional voice) control over sessions, jobs and worktrees
candidates.description: A `/control` (Puck-style) agent that can list/inspect/spawn/steer/stop threads, daemon jobs, teams and worktrees — 'spawn an agent in worktree X to fix the CI failure', 'archive finished threads', 'what is job 7 waiting on' — implemented as tools over the existing dashboard, threads, jobs and team registries; voice input via injected STT as a later step.
candidates.competitor: Amp Puck (Jul 20) + Talk to Puck (Aug 18); Grok Build dashboard; Warp Agents bar drill-down (Aug 13)
candidates.why_killer: Managing ten parallel agents stops being a keyboard-navigation problem: the user says what should happen to which run and it happens. v1 #11 (Mission Control) shipped only the watch half; a control agent is the fastest way to ship the control half, and it reuses the team/ledger/daemon APIs instead of a bespoke UI.

candidates.title: Fast spawn: content-store clone, branch-tip fetch, linked-worktree reuse and prebuilt environment snapshots
candidates.description: When teams/best-of-N/daemon create worktrees or sandboxes: reuse a matching local checkout as a linked worktree, fetch only the branch tip by default, keep a local content store so repeated clones are near-instant, and let sandbox.toml declare a build step whose result is snapshotted and reused so agents start with dependencies installed.
candidates.competitor: Grok Build `grok clone` content store / linked-worktree reuse (1.0.6, 1.0.10); Cursor Builds 3x faster start (Aug 13)
candidates.why_killer: Best-of-5 or an eight-teammate fan-out starts in seconds rather than waiting on five `npm install`s, which is what makes parallelism cheap enough to use by default. Competitors moved this bar in August; bog's parallel-worktree and sandbox factory paths are where it plugs in, and the daemon benefits on every trigger.

candidates.title: Governed multi-harness workers: run Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build as sub-agents under bog's rules, ledger and evidence
candidates.description: A `HarnessSubAgentBackend` that launches an external CLI in headless mode (Anthropic stream-json / Codex exec / Grok headless), maps its tool events onto bog's hook bus so Expert Mode, SafeTools, DLP and CostLedger apply to each tool call, and folds its result into the team ledger and evidence bundle; selectable per pipeline stage.
candidates.competitor: Warp Oz/Factories multi-harness control plane (May 20; Aug 27); Cursor cloud harness
candidates.why_killer: A team keeps the harness each developer already loves while security gets one policy engine, one audit trail and one cost cap across all of them — the value Warp charges enterprises for, delivered as a self-hosted Python package. Grok Build's headless output is wire-compatible with Anthropic stream-json (per the July review), so two of three harnesses share one adapter.

candidates.title: Incremental self-review with reviewed-diff memo, effort levels and CI dedupe
candidates.description: `/self-review` remembers the hash of the last reviewed diff per branch, reviews only what changed since, exposes default/high/custom effort (custom = natural-language rule for when to go deep), and the headless twin leaves a 'already reviewed this diff' marker so a CI run skips the repeat.
candidates.competitor: Cursor Bugbot June update: /review pre-push, diff dedupe, incremental review, effort levels (Jun 10)
candidates.why_killer: A developer who ran the review locally is not charged and not nagged again when the same diff lands in the PR, and follow-up pushes get feedback only on the new hunks. v1 #3 shipped self-review with five lenses; Bugbot moved the bar to incremental + deduped + effort-graded, all of which are cheap on top of bog's existing controller and rubric grader.

candidates.title: Live preview portals: port-forwarded, shareable preview URLs for agent-built apps (local tunnel or daemon-hosted)
candidates.description: When a run starts a dev server in a sandbox/worktree/worker, expose it as a preview with a friendly name (localhost tunnel for solo, daemon-hosted reverse proxy with auth for teams), link it from the turn-end tray and evidence bundle, and let the browser/QA tools use it for verification.
candidates.competitor: Amp Portals (Aug 6) + friendly URLs (Aug 23); Cursor no-repo start with browser preview + Vercel publish (Aug 27)
candidates.why_killer: A teammate or PM clicks one link to see what the agent built instead of checking out the branch, and the evidence bundle can include a live URL rather than a stale screenshot. Both cloud competitors now treat previews as part of 'done'; bog's `/preview` and `/qa` surfaces need a novelty check before scoping.

candidates.title: Desktop-in-sandbox and computer use on self-hosted workers, including Windows desktops
candidates.description: Expose an interactive desktop (Linux via Xvfb/noVNC in sandboxes; Windows via the worker's own session) so agents can drive GUI apps, record verification video, and let humans peek in; gate by trust profile and record to the evidence bundle.
candidates.competitor: Amp Desktop in orbs (Sep 4); Cursor computer use on Linux/Mac self-hosted workers (Sep 2); Warp computer-use recordings
candidates.why_killer: Teams shipping desktop or Windows-native software get an agent that can actually open the app it just built and prove it works — and nobody offers computer use on a Windows worker today. Depends on the worker-pool candidate; sequence after it.

market_trends: Always-on is the new default: in one summer Cursor (subscriptions, /goal, persist), Amp (event-driven orbs, self-scheduling), Grok Build (Workflows, timer scripts) and Warp (Factories) all reframed the agent as a long-lived service that wakes on events and holds a goal, so a terminal agent that only runs while a human watches now reads as last-generation.

Execution is moving to where the code lives while orchestration stays hosted: Cursor Self-Hosted Machines, Warp Factories in-VPC, Amp orbs and `oz runner` all split 'agent loop in the cloud, tools on your machines' — and none of them ships a Windows worker.

Model routing became a product feature with a cost objective (Cursor Router's Intelligence/Balance/Cost, Warp custom routers, Amp's Dial with an open-weight low tier), and 'who cares about the model' (Amp, Jul 29) is now a stated strategy — the harness, not the model, is where vendors claim differentiation.

Pricing converged on subscription-plus-included-usage with metered overage (Cursor Pro/Pro+/Ultra and Teams Premium, Amp Megawatt/Gigawatt, Warp Build/Max, Grok inside SuperGrok) while free tiers shrank or closed (Amp Free closed, Warp free credits tapered), and BYOK / linked third-party subscriptions became the standard escape hatch that bog's local-model and BYOK posture already satisfies.

Trust became a release feature: Grok Build's whole-repo upload scandal forced an Apache-2.0 source drop within 72 hours (with contributions closed), Warp open-sourced its client under AGPL, and Cursor markets 'never initiates a connection into your network' — users now ask what leaves the machine, and a verifiable answer is a differentiator.

Consolidation and vendor risk are real: SpaceX now owns both xAI and Cursor, OpenAI is cutting Cursor off on 2026-11-12, Anthropic chose to stay — multi-provider neutrality and self-hosting are selling points precisely because the largest IDE-agent vendor lost some of both.

Proof beats diff: Amp's Fable 5.1 framing, Cursor's merge-ready cloud PRs and Warp's computer-use recordings all attach evidence (video, screenshots, metrics) to agent output, and review surfaces are being redesigned around it (intelligently ordered diffs, incremental Bugbot).

Fan-out scale is now a headline number (Grok 128-1,024 agents per workflow, Grok 1.0's 8 worktree subagents, Amp agent-to-agent, Cursor isolated-VM subagents) which makes hard budgets, spawn caps and per-agent cost attribution table stakes rather than governance extras.

Commoditized in this window: plan mode, /rewind, MCP with OAuth, skills/plugins marketplaces, subagents in worktrees, Slack integration, voice input, terminal image rendering, and headless/CI modes — none of these differentiates any longer.

Interop layers are settling around headless wire formats and multi-harness control planes (Warp running Claude Code/Codex/Cursor, Grok's Anthropic stream-json compatibility, ACP for editors), so being a governed host for other harnesses is a bigger opportunity than being one more harness.
